article_title: M&S replaces plastic with paper packaging across men’s essentials range
sub_title: Marks & Spencer is switching to FSC-certified paper for its men’s socks, pyjama sets, and selected underwear.
article_content: As part of its Plan A roadmap to achieve net zero by 2040, Marks & Spencer has reinforced its commitment to reducing plastic packaging by switching to FSC-certified paper for its men’s socks, pyjama sets, and selected underwear. The change, which includes paper hooks instead of plastic, will see the British retailer remove almost 5.5 million units of plastic from its clothing and home business over the next year. With one in five men in the UK purchasing their underwear and nightwear from M&S, and with 20 million pairs of men’s socks sold by the retailer each year, Marks & Spencer said it is focused on ensuring its packaging is easily recyclable for customers. Katharine Beacham, Head of Sustainability in Clothing & Home at M&S, said: "We know we have a responsibility to do the right thing when it comes to our packaging by reducing unnecessary plastic. "This one small change to our men’s essentials range will make a huge difference by removing over five million units of plastic from our supply chain. "It also gives our customers the confidence to make more sustainable choices more easily when they shop with us, and trust that the M&S quality products they love are made, sourced and packaged with care."

article_title: By Rotation brings bridal rentals starting at £9 to Mayfair pop-up
sub_title: If you fall into the category of people who don't believe in spending big bucks on a wedding or bridesmaid dress that'll...
article_content: If you fall into the category of people who don't believe in spending big bucks on a wedding or bridesmaid dress that'll only be worn once, then fashion rental platform By Rotation may have the answer to your fashion and price point prayers. By Rotation has launched a limited-time Bridal Suite in its Mayfair pop-up 'House of ByRo'. The average wedding dress costs £1,500, but what if you could get your dream gown for a fraction of the price? Rental house By Rotation is offering alternatives for those who truly want to step into the tradition of "something borrowed" with prices starting from as little as £9. Founded by Eshita Kabra-Davies in 2019, By Rotation has been revolutionising fashion consumption "by empowering users to rent, lend, and rotate their wardrobes". With over a million downloads and 150,000 listings in the UK and US, the business has grown to become a leader in the sustainable fashion movement. The Bridal Suite has been curated to serve those planning a wedding or any special occasion, with the option to rent everything from accessories to ready-to-wear. Guests can book a complimentary appointment to browse and rent from a curated selection of high-end bridalwear, including pieces from coveted designers such as Roksanda, 16Arlington, Taller Marmo, Self-Portrait and Victoria Beckham. Those booking in will be presented with a personalised rail of rental options tailored to the original booking request and complimentary champagne courtesy of the champagne house Mumm. All rentals will also come with a complimentary Who Is Elijah perfume. Eshita Kabra-Davies, Founder of By Rotation, told TheIndustry.fashion: "We are thrilled to bring the By Rotation Bridal Suite to life at our Mayfair pop-up. "Bridalwear is one of the most significant investments someone can make, and we are proud to offer a more sustainable and affordable alternative that aligns with our commitment to conscious consumption." Eshita Kabra-Davies, Founder of By Rotation The Bridal Suite is housed at the brand's Mayfair pop-up, which is also the "world’s largest" fashion rental pop-up. The five-story space at 31 Brook Street, which opened its doors in October , showcases the brand’s most popular garments and accessories, "creating an immersive and interactive retail experience".

article_title: Editors' Top Reads: News from John Lewis, Topshop and London College of Fashion
sub_title: Here are some of this week’s news and features highlights handpicked by TheIndustry.fashion team.
article_content: Here are some of this week’s news and features highlights handpicked by TheIndustry.fashion team. If you're in your late 20s, you'll know Topshop wasn’t just a fashion brand - it was a movement. Take it from me, a Millennial, who was in her teenage prime during Topshop's heyday. For many Millennials, like myself, it was the backdrop to formative fashion moments: the first pair of skinny jeans, the hunt for the perfect party dress, the pilgrimage to Oxford Circus. But as the high street continues to evolve and Topshop prepares for its comeback under new ownership, it’s facing a much more complex landscape - and a new generation of shoppers who may not hold the same nostalgic ties. Last month, Topshop took to social media platform Instagram with a series of three posts that spelled out "We've missed you too". This was the confirmation that fans of Topshop had all been waiting for: it's back. So far, it's looking likely that the beloved British retailer is headed back to the high street, but which one, however, remains a mystery. As its new owner, Bestseller, prepares to make waves in the industry, I am bracing myself for its return. Can it live up to my nostalgic memories? Will I ever relive the days of Topshop's Joni jeans and John Lennon emblazoned tees? I spoke to fashion and retail experts to get their opinions on whether Topshop can take back the high street and how it needs to go about appealing to its OG customers as well as garnering Gen Zers. Read the full feature here to see what they had to say . Chloé Burney, Senior New & Features Writer. It was good to hear that John Lewis is rolling out its repair service to all of its UK stores this week , following a successful trial in five stores last summer. The service will continue to be in partnership with Johnsons, a Timpson Group company, offering fashion repairs, alterations, dry cleaning and even handbag restoration. I’m keen to give it a go at some point as I always seem to have something old knocking about in my wardrobe that I’d like to give new life to with a mend, or something new (albeit not very often these days!) that needs a slight alteration before it gets a debut wearing. I do hope it is clearly signposted in-store at my nearest John Lewis in Kingston and that it is a swift and not too expensive service, as the chap I use locally for any mends and alterations seems to have seriously hiked up his prices this year. It’s made me reluctant to use him, or certainly think twice, which is not great as I do like to support local independent businesses where I can. Maybe the cost is a widespread issue for people, as indicated by John Lewis also reporting that it is seeing a trend of increasing interest in at-home repairs, with haberdashery accessories up 36% year-on-year and searches for sewing machines up 50%. Or maybe it’s ‘The Great British Sewing Bee’ effect, which would be timely as series 11 starts on BBC One next month! Tom Bottomley, Contributing Editor. I first discovered Sophie Tea on TikTok, watching her transform charity shop finds into bold, expressive art. So, when her name popped up in collaboration with the London College of Fashion (LCF) in the search for the UK’s next circular fashion stars, I was instantly intrigued. As part of its Young Creators series, Visa has teamed up with Tea and the London College of Fashion to launch the ‘Recycle the Runway’ initiative . This exciting project will award six talented finalists, including one grand prize winner, with individual grants from a total prize pool of £20,000. The aim? To encourage creators to reimagine how they design, produce and sell fashion, making re-commerce (the regenerative way to buy, re-use and share goods and services) "desirable and habitual to accelerate economic growth". Finalists will present their collections at a catwalk show in London on 22 May, judged by Tea alongside experts from Visa and the British fashion industry. I look forward to hearing about the winners! Sophie Smith, News Editor & Senior Writer.

article_title: John Lewis rolls out repair service to all UK stores
sub_title: John Lewis is rolling out its repair service to all UK stores this week, following a "hugely successful" trial that launched in just five stores in July 2024.
article_content: John Lewis is rolling out its repair service to all UK stores this week, following a "hugely successful" trial that launched in just five stores in July 2024. The service will continue to be in partnership with Johnsons, a Timpson Group company, offering fashion repairs, alterations, dry cleaning and handbag restoration. Katie Papakonstantinou, Director of Services & Hospitality at John Lewis, said: "We’re so excited to bring this service to all John Lewis stores. John Lewis has always been committed to providing a brilliant retail experience for customers, and repair adds another dimension to that. "The great thing about repair is it works for the old and the new. Whether you need something tailored to fit you better or want to give your mum’s old handbag a new life, we’ve made it easy to restore treasured products." Marija Rompani, Director of Ethics & Sustainability for John Lewis Partnership, added: "We’re still learning about which circular economy models work, so it’s great when a trial delivers positive results and shows us how we can make it effective at scale. "Repair is a crucial part of the circular economy and mirrors our commitment to designing items with quality and longevity in mind, as part of our circular strategy." The most popular services from the trial were minor rip and seam repairs, indicating that customers are "looking to fix wear and tear of their beloved everyday items", as well trouser alterations for those looking for a better fit. According to John Lewis, a major success of the initial trial was the restoration of a vintage Chanel bag to near new condition within days. From today, 9 April, customers are able to drop off their much loved items to be cleaned, repaired or altered at their local John Lewis shop, and My John Lewis loyalty members will be able to claim 5% off all single repair services as a continuous offer. Additionally, John Lewis is also seeing a trend of increasing interest in at-home repairs, with haberdashery accessories up 36% year-on-year and searches for John Lewis sewing machines up 50% year-on-year. The retailer also says that the search for ‘pink sewing machines’ is up 255%, as customers look to purchase machines as gifts and prolong the life of their much-loved products at home.

article_title: Visa teams up with LCF and Sophie Tea to search for UK’s next circular fashion stars
sub_title: Visa has teamed up with the London College of Fashion and artist and social media star, Sophie Tea, on a new initiative...
article_content: Visa has partnered with the London College of Fashion (LCF) and artist and social media star, Sophie Tea, on a new initiative to help accelerate the business growth of budding circular fashion entrepreneurs in the UK. As part of its Visa Young Creators series, the ‘Recycle the Runway’ initiative will see six successful finalists, including one grand prize winner, receive individual grants from a total prize pool of £20,000. They will also receive access to mentoring from industry experts during the competition, as well as the opportunity to be recognised by fashion industry body, London College of Fashion, UAL. Finalists will present their collections at a catwalk show in Central London on 22 May 2025, judged by Sophie Tea alongside experts from Visa and the British fashion industry. Visa’s aim is to encourage creators to reimagine how they design, produce and sell fashion, making recommerce – the regenerative way to buy, re-use and share goods and services – "desirable and habitual to accelerate economic growth". Katherine Brown, VP, Head of Social Impact & Sustainability at Visa Europe, said: "Recommerce is more than a buzzword, it’s a powerful shift in how we buy and sell goods, which is driving growth in the UK economy. "Through our Recycle the Runway initiative, we’re excited to celebrate fashion creators who are embracing this change and to help provide the tools they need to grow through circular business models. By making circular fashion more accessible, and rewarding, we can help these small businesses thrive." Sophie Tea, who is known for her distinctive and inclusive paintings, added: "Creativity has always been my thing - taking ideas and turning them into something real and meaningful. I love a story, and that’s why I’m so excited to be part of the Visa Creators Recycle the Runway initiative. "It’s an amazing chance for creators to bring their talent to life while celebrating those who make reusing and repurposing a priority. "This initiative is all about reimagining how we create, wear, and give a second life to fashion. If you’re a designer who’s committed to conscious design, this is your moment to get noticed, learn from the best, and level up your business. I’m so looking forward to seeing all the brilliant ideas that come through." The closing date for entrants is 8 May 2025 and applicants must be at least 18 years of age and based in the UK to enter. They must also have an early stage start-up business with a minimum of one year in operation, and they must also be able to demonstrate how their design-led business embraces circular business models to align with at least one of the ‘R’s of circular fashion; repair, resale, return, redistribution, rental or refill.

article_title: 'House of Vinted' luxury fashion launches online following London pop-up
sub_title: Vinted is today launching its second-hand luxury fashion concept, ‘House of Vinted’, online following its ‘by invitation only’ pop-up at The Adria Hotel in London last weekend – its first ‘in real life’ event - from 6pm this evening.
article_content: Vinted is today launching its second-hand luxury fashion concept, ‘House of Vinted’, online following its 'by invitation only' pop-up at The Adria Hotel in London last weekend - its first ‘in real life’ event - from 6pm this evening. Vinted members will be able to shop online for designer items from brands including Gucci, Prada, Maison Margiela, Jacquemus and The Row, curated by ‘fashion creators’ including Susie Lau, Victoria Magrath, Simran Randhawa, Giulia Valentina and Keiona Revlon – with most pieces coming directly from their personal wardrobes. The themes of the wardrobes are not only based on the styles of the creators involved, but also on Vinted data which shows there is an increasing trend for search terms like ‘art deco’, ‘gingham’, ‘vintage’, ‘scandi’, ‘statement piece’, ‘puff sleeves’ and ‘cable knit sweaters’. Highlights from Susie Lau’s wardrobe include a Prada SS20 dress, a Comme des Garçons ‘Tricot’ silver skirt, which she bought on one of her vintage shopping trips to Tokyo, and a pair of Maison Margiela ‘Tabi’ shoes. Victoria Magrath’s wardrobe favourites up for sale include a blue Balmain suit which she wore to the launch of her book ‘The New Fashion Rules’, a pair of Valentino platform heels - which she wore when Valentino Beauty took her to Rome for a launch, and a pair of Balmain x H&M heels, which she "queued up for hours outside the Manchester store" to get her hands on. Emma Sullivan, Creative Director at Vinted, said: "Following our 'House of Vinted' showcase in London last weekend, from today Vinted members across the UK will be able to shop items from the specially curated wardrobes seen at the event. "I am excited for our members to share in the joy that comes from buying and selling luxury second-hand fashion." Creator Susie Lau said: "I don’t often sell things as I’m quite attached to most of my wardrobe, but I loved the idea of curating a collection and bringing that pre-loved experience to life." Fellow creator Victoria Magrath added: "Vinted has long been my preferred platform for selling pre-loved luxury pieces and designer items. I shall be selling several pieces that have held a special meaning to me, inspired by the concept of ‘Art Deco Déjà vu’. "I can’t wait for people to experience the collections and for the items to become new again in someone else’s closet." Part of the proceeds from the House of Vinted wardrobe sale will go to Oxfam, though it’s not clear how much.

article_title: Traceable Tod’s brings Digital Product Passports to its iconic Gommino footwear
sub_title: Tod’s, the luxury footwear brand renowned for its Gommino loafers and driving shoes, is introducing Digital Product Passports...
article_content: Tod’s, the luxury footwear brand renowned for its Gommino loafers and driving shoes, is introducing Digital Product Passports (DPP) to all footwear it's renowned for. Building on the successful implementation of DPPs for the custom Di Bag, this latest expansion – in collaboration with Aura’s blockchain technology - underscores Tod’s commitment to enhancing traceability and authenticity for their consumers. So, what exactly are DPPs? In recent years, the fashion industry has been criticised for a lack of transparency, and part of the problem has been a lack of standardised information. A Digital Product Passport is a digital record that provides information about a product and its value chain from its inception to landing on local shelves. This includes everything from the origin of the product, materials used, environmental impact and disposal recommendations. Trials have seen retailers print barcodes on the labels of garments, which are scanned to reveal the above information. After learning about a product's environmental impact, customers can then make informed choices about where they want to shop. Through Tod's collaboration with Aura and Temera, customers will now be able to scan the embedded NFC chip located in the right sole of their My Gommino loafers. The chip and underlying traceability solution, meaning that customers can register their products and claim ownership directly through their smartphones. This process also grants customers access to an authenticity certificate. Beyond certification, Tod’s also offers unique additional features, such as engaging storytelling elements to their DPP. It'll also include details and insights on the many artisans and craftspeople that create each My Gommino loafer. Carlo Alberto Beretta, Tod’s General Brand Manager, said: "At Tod’s, we view the DPP as more than just a tool for product authentication and traceability. Though these are critically important elements, we also want to take the opportunity to deepen our connection with customers, showcase our craftmanship, and elevate the storytelling of our iconic products." Tod’s Digital Passports are also tools to elevate the customer experience. Via the scannable barcode, customers have access to extended warranty and Tod’s care, a dedicated client advisor, exclusive events and more. Romain Carrere, CEO of Aura Blockchain Consortium, commented: "We are pleased to announce the continuation of our collaboration with Tod’s. By ambitiously extending its DPP offering beyond the custom Di Bag, and with engaging story-telling capabilities, Tod’s is reaffirming that transparency, authenticity and customer experience can go hand in hand, like never before." Read TheIndustry.fashion's feature 'Everything you need to know about Digital Product Passport' to learn more.

article_title: Beyond Retro’s parent company partners with Coach to bring upcycling to luxury sector
sub_title: Bank & Vogue, the parent company of vintage clothing chain Beyond Retro, has partnered with American luxury...
article_content: Bank & Vogue, the parent company of vintage clothing chain Beyond Retro, has partnered with American luxury fashion house Coach on a limited-edition collection of bags crafted from repurposed textiles. Transforming pre-loved denim and leather into high-end accessories, the new sustainability-driven collaboration aims to bring upcycling and circularity to the luxury sector, with bags retailing on the Coach website and in selected stores for £395 - £730. Key pieces include the patchwork ‘Cargo Tote Bag’, described as “a spacious and lightweight carry-all crafted from love-worn denim garments”. It features Coach’s signature glove-tanned leather, cursive Coach script embroidery, and its iconic turn-lock closure. Designed with function in mind, it has an open interior that fits a 13” laptop, two external pockets and a removable webbing strap. There’s also the ‘Tabby Shoulder Bag 26’ with patchwork quilting, which reimagines the classic Coach ‘Tabby’ bag, and the ‘Rogue Patchwork Denim Top-Handle Bag’ which blends Coach’s ‘Rogue’ bag structured silhouette with a unique patchwork of repurposed denim. Steven Bethell, Co-Founder of Beyond Retro and Bank & Vogue, which is one of the largest wholesalers of pre-loved textiles in the world, said: "The partnership developed out of a mutual commitment to sustainability and circular fashion. "Bank & Vogue is experienced in sourcing and repurposing post-consumer textiles. Coach sought to leverage this expertise to integrate sustainable practices into its luxury offerings, leading to this collaboration. "The bags are made from post-consumer denim sourced by Bank & Vogue. These denim materials typically come from discarded jeans that aren't suitable for resale. They're carefully sorted, cut into components (pattern pieces), and then sent to Coach’s finished goods factory to seamlessly fit into their production processes. "These bags are for everyone who wants a beautiful looking bag with the added bonus of it being circular and kinder to the planet."

article_title: Why The Handbag Clinic is committing to Selfridges with preloved pop-ups across UK
sub_title: The Handbag Clinic, the handbag restorer and luxury reseller, is expanding its partnership with Selfridges, bringing pop-ups...
article_content: The Handbag Clinic, the handbag restorer and luxury reseller, is expanding its partnership with Selfridges, bringing pop-ups to Birmingham and Manchester later this month. You may have recalled The Handbag Clinic opening up a concession at Harrods' hallowed halls back in 2023, which closed after 6 months. The luxury reseller switched things up, opening a permanent in-store concession at the rival luxury department store, Selfridges London, in April 2024. According to The Handbag Clinic’s CEO and co-founder, Charlotte Staerck, "After launching The Handbag Clinic’s permanent home in Selfridges London’s Reselfridges in March 2024, we evaluated our retail portfolio and felt that Selfridges – with its exceptional commitment to circularity – is much more aligned with our proposition." Now, it is bringing its circular offering of ‘Buy, Sell, Restore, Authenticate’ to Selfridges Manchester Trafford on 21-23 March, followed by Selfridges Birmingham on 28-30 March. The Handbag Clinic’s pop-up, set within the Reselfridges edit, will showcase the "ultimate next-level circularity model" from buying to selling and even restoring preloved pieces. So, why not unlock the power of your wardrobe? Shoppers are invited to trade in their unwanted luxury handbags, regardless of where they were purchased, in exchange for a Selfridges gift voucher to spend in-store. It will also stock a handpicked collection of fully authenticated, preowned luxury handbags from coveted brands including Fendi, Balenciaga, Chanel and more. Plus,  for any purchases at the pop-ups, customers can take advantage of The Handbag Clinic’s ‘Circle Back’ programme – guaranteeing a buy-back for up to 12 months post-purchase. Repair and restoration services are also available, spanning all luxury leather goods from handbags to trainers and even leather clothing. Prices start from £95 for minor stitch work and go right through to £600+ for more complex restorations. Staerck said: "We are so excited to be building on our partnership with Selfridges to bring The Handbag Clinic to an even wider community of luxury enthusiasts. "Manchester and Birmingham are two of the most exciting shopping destinations in the UK and home to discerning communities of luxury investors. They understand that true circularity begins with what we already have in our wardrobes. By repairing these items and prolonging their lifespan, or by trading them in, they can continue to get their newness fix whilst being kind to their wallets and the planet." The Handbag Clinic operates through its e-commerce platform and in-store concessions across London, Newcastle, Colchester and York as well as at Selfridges London.

article_title: Editors' Top Reads: News from Versace, PrettyLittleThing, Gabicci and more...
sub_title: Here are some of this week’s news and features highlights handpicked by TheIndustry.fashion team.
article_content: Here are some of this week’s news and features highlights handpicked by TheIndustry.fashion team. I never thought I'd see the day that Donatella Versace stepped down from Versace's helm. But, then again, I never thought I'd see the day Gucci would appoint Demna as its Artistic Director. Alas, both have become realities in this week's game of Creative Director chess. This week, Versace announced that Donatella Versace, its Chief Creative Officer, will be transitioning to the role of Chief Brand Ambassador after 27 years at the helm of the brand that her late brother Gianni Versace founded in 1978. In her new role as Chief Brand Ambassador, effective 1 April, Donatella Versace will dedicate herself to the support of the brand's philanthropic and charitable endeavours and will "remain an advocate for the brand globally". But who would dare take Donatella's spot? Dario Vitale. And who is the new Chief Creative Officer, Dario Vitale? After graduating from Insitiuto Marangoni in 2006, the now 41-year-old went to work at Dsquared2 for a year before joining Bottega Veneta. In 2010, he packed his bags and headed to Miu Miu, where he worked his way up to Design & Image Director. Since rumours began swirling that he was leaving the brand after 15 years, the industry waited to see if Vitale would head to Bottega Veneta, Gucci or Versace. As the first non-Versace family member to helm the luxury Italian label, let's see if he's cut from the same Medussa-printed cloth. Chloé Burney, Senior News & Features Writer. The urgency of sustainable consumption has forced a reckoning within the fast fashion industry. PrettyLittleThing and Boohoo Group, synonymous with rapid trend cycles and low prices, are now attempting to reposition themselves. The question remains: do these rebrands signal a genuine shift in their business models, or are they carefully crafted narratives designed to appeal to environmentally conscious consumers? Last week, PrettyLittleThing revealed a rebrand that promises to take the brand far beyond its fast fashion roots. Under the guidance of co-founder Umar Kamani, who rejoined the company in September 2024, PLT is positioning itself with a new ethos: 'A Legacy in Progress'. Meanwhile, Boohoo Group has announced its rebrand to the Debenhams Group. These moves come at a time when consumer demand is increasingly leaning toward slower fashion as shoppers begin to rethink the environmental impact of their purchases. Our News & Features Writer, Chloé Burney, explores what PLT and Boohoo's rebrands say about fast fashion , with commentary from industry experts on the moves. Sophie Smith, News Editor & Senior Writer. I do love a decent ‘collector gets hands on deadstock haul’ story, and this week saw Gabicci come up with the goods. An old menswear store in Paris closed down due to the death of the owner and, after much time had elapsed, a clearance Sale saw a load of original 1970s Gabicci tops - still in original packaging – unearthed. Somehow, UK collector Chris Alexander managed to get his hands on some and subsequently approached Gabicci with them. The result is a new Gabicci Archive collection which, near as damn it, has replicated the originals , albeit in a different but considered viscose and nylon mix fabric (as the original acetate fabric is no longer used for legal reasons). Gabicci even purchased a new machine in order to make the larger knitted collars as they originally were. What is perhaps unusual is, collectors rarely like to lend such items to the brand that originally made them, in return for a new top and not much else as far as I can gather. They’ve had a real touch there. There was a teaser piece launched in a previous season, but the first main Gabicci Archive collection of five pieces, replicated in two original colours – with 100 per piece per colour – launched in retro-focused menswear stores this week, and they have apparently been flying out. There’s more to come for AW25 too. Tom Bottomley, Contributing Editor. Who said “Time is money”? Luxury retailers now want both. No longer content with just enticing the money from your credit card, they want your precious free time too. With physical retail having a renaissance, dwell time is becoming increasingly important to retailers and they would like you to stay longer, measuring success and engagement on the amount of time people spend in their stores. Retailers are increasingly focusing on the quality of the customer experience, rewarding shoppers for their time rather than just their spending, as Marcus Jaye explores in his recent column for TheIndustry.fashion . He points to Printemps' innovative approach in New York, where success is measured by leisure time spent, and Selfridges' updated rewards scheme, which now recognises and incentivises in-store engagement. This shift signals a move towards creating immersive and enjoyable shopping environments.

article_title: Vinted to launch second-hand luxury fashion pop-up in London
sub_title: Pre-loved fashion marketplace Vinted is launching its first-ever second-hand luxury fashion pop-up in London on 22 March.
article_content: Pre-loved fashion marketplace Vinted is launching its first-ever second-hand luxury fashion pop-up in London on 22 March at The Adria hotel, 88 Queen’s Gate in South Kensington, called ‘House of Vinted’. By invitation only, Vinted members will be able to explore themed rooms with curated wardrobes from international luxury style creators including Susie Lau , Victoria Magrath , Simran Randhawa , Giulia Valentina and Keiona Revlon . Each room will feature fashion pieces and accessories sourced through Vinted, from Vinted’s archives or from the creators’ own personal wardrobes. The wardrobes include brands such as Prada, Gucci, Maison Margiela, Jacquemus and The Row. The different themed rooms will offer a distinct ‘past-forward’ experience, including ‘Art Deco Déjà Vu’, ‘Modern Eclectic’s Encore’ and ‘Cottagecore Comeback’. Emma Sullivan, Creative Director at Vinted, said: "The House of Vinted is not just a unique opportunity to browse luxury pieces, it's a celebration of the stories behind pre-loved luxury fashion. "By making luxury accessible and affordable, Vinted invites guests to discover the timeless beauty of lived-in luxury, encouraging them to rewrite their own fashion stories with these cherished items. "Everything about the House of Vinted is designed to make guests look and feel ‘new again’ - from rediscovering iconic items from epochs-past, to bringing back trends from decades ago, as well as getting hot tips from luxury creators." Visitors will also be able to relax and refuel in a Vinted café, which will serve cold-pressed juices and a selection of sweet and savoury treats. Additionally, the pop-up space will offer workshops including leather embossing and a ‘Luxury Style Surgery’ where guests can seek professional styling advice from stylist and wardrobe consultant, Manisha Sabharwal . As attendance is by invitation and registration only, Vinted members are advised to keep an eye out in their email inbox for an invite to House of Vinted. For those Vinted members who miss the pop-up experience, certain items will be available to buy from a dedicated House of Vinted website page from 25 March, with part of the proceeds going to Oxfam UK.

article_title: In My View by Eric Musgrave: Giving Scottish heritage a future
sub_title: We can expect “a tsunami of job cuts” across UK clothing and textile factories later this year thanks to the imposition of higher operating costs in
article_content: We can expect “a tsunami of job cuts” across UK clothing and textile factories later this year thanks to the imposition of higher operating costs in Labour’s Budget last autumn against the backdrop of continuing challenging trading conditions in almost all the world’s leading markets. This was the gloomy prediction I received from a Scottish factory owner during the Pitti Uomo menswear fair in January. His downbeat assessment was a rare cloud in what was, for me, a rather uplifting and inspiring event. Given what I wrote about the effects of the Budget in my January column I cannot claim to be surprised by my contact’s remark but the depth of pain he inferred was very concerning. With all this going on, therefore, it’s very pleasant for me to highlight a UK textile success story, or more precisely a Scottish one. The Glenlyon Tweed Mill in Aberfeldy, Perthshire was acquired in November by the team that owns Stewart Christie in Edinburgh, Scotland’s oldest bespoke tailor and a revival of a 200-year-old weaving business is now underway. My long-standing friends Victoria “Vixy” Rae and Daniel Fearn are the business partners who took on Stewart Christie almost 10 years ago and have carefully revived and repositioned the business without losing any of the old-school charm that makes it so appealing to a certain type of consumer (like me!) who enjoys quality clothes and quality service. The pair now plan to do the same with the mill, which boasts an enviable heritage. Up until 2012 it was the production unit for the celebrated country tweeds of Haggart of Aberfeldy, a legendary name in the niche world of robust Scottish cloths. When the company went bust, the Haggart name went elsewhere and appears to have disappeared from the market but the mill continued in a very small way as Glenlyon Tweed Mill, producing the type of cloth needed and appreciated by country estate gamekeepers and country estate owners alike. In February I had an enjoyable couple of days introducing Glenlyon’s cloths to a good number of London bespoke tailors on and off Savile Row, plus a few upmarket ready-to-wear producers that would appreciate their quality. I was accompanied by Isaac Hawkins, a cheerful 30-year-old who is the on-site kilt maker at Stewart Christie. An excellent example of the sort of young people who are embracing old craft skills as a career option, Isaac is very enthusiastic about the opportunity to learn about the arcane techniques of high-quality weaving and is splitting his time between the shop in Edinburgh and the mill in Aberfeldy, around 75 miles to the north-west. We received a very positive response from most of the tailors we visited for the samples we carried with us. Certainly the classic 700gm / 25oz gamekeeper tweeds have distinctly niche appeal, but the lighter, softer qualities in 500gm / 18oz and 350gm / 12oz prompted many favourable comments and quite a few orders. I wish Vixy and Dan and their business partners all the best in their new venture. I am confident they will find an appropriate niche for Glenlyon Tweed Mill but this is but a small ray of sunshine in a tough time for UK textiles. As the mill has only been ticking over for more than a decade, the new owners inherited only two workers, both with many years’ experience. The big challenge now will be to attract younger talent to ensure the expertise and skills of Scottish weavers is not diluted or lost. As I have written many times in the past, a problem for my depressed Scottish friend at Pitti Uomo and my more confident pals at Glenlyon is that British manufacturers of textiles, clothing, footwear and accessories are, relatively speaking, so little known and so little appreciated by most of the general population and a hell of a lot of people in the fashion business. It is a precious industry hidden right under our noses. I fear the reality in the foreseeable future is that most UK manufacturers will survive only as niche specialists – maybe that’s the situation already. It all makes me rather sad. On a much more positive note, the inaugural People, Planet and Purpose Awards event held by theindustry.fashion in London on 27th February was a very enjoyable celebration of the work of quite a few young companies that are navigating the tricky waters of contemporary fashion. I had a great time meeting up with friends old and new. I salute Lauretta Roberts and Antony Hawman for devising a format that was different to the familiar industry awards. Here’s to the next one. I doubt even my powers of persuasion could get them to bring in more UK textiles-relevant categories for next year, but I might try.

article_title: What PrettyLittleThing and Boohoo's rebrands say about fast fashion
sub_title: In a world where sustainability is no longer a trend but a necessity, two of the UK's biggest fast fashion giants...
article_content: In a world where sustainability is no longer a trend but a necessity, two of the UK's biggest fast fashion giants, PrettyLittleThing and Boohoo , are rewriting their stories. Once the go-to brands for affordable, trend-led styles, they’re now trying to reinvent themselves — but are these rebrands a genuine shift or just a clever marketing move? Once dominant players in the fast fashion market, both PLT and Boohoo have announced significant rebrands, signalling a potential shift in their places within the industry. These moves come at a time when consumer demand is increasingly leaning toward slower fashion as shoppers begin to rethink the environmental impact of their purchases. Last week, PrettyLittleThing revealed a rebrand that promises to take the brand far beyond its fast fashion roots. Now, under the guidance of co-founder Umar Kamani, who rejoined the company in September 2024, PLT is positioning itself with a new ethos: 'A Legacy in Progress'. Kamani emphasised that the rebrand isn’t just a cosmetic change but a cultural shift that aims to redefine accessible luxury for a new generation. He said: "We are leaving ‘fast fashion’ as we currently know it behind." The co-founder noted that the focus is now on producing elevated styles that have longevity in both design and wear. The aim is clear: to offer consumers high-quality, timeless pieces that can be worn repeatedly, resisting the unsustainable cycle of purchasing items for single-use occasions. However, the road ahead isn’t without challenges. Chloe Collins, Head of Apparel at GlobalData, points out that PLT’s attempt to reposition itself with more "elevated, timeless styles" is unlikely to fully address the challenges the brand faces. "The rise of Shein, with its ultra-low prices and swift reaction to trends, has made it almost impossible for fellow fast fashion brands to keep up", said Collins. She also highlighted the growing shift among young shoppers towards more sustainable options. This is a far cry from the disposable, trend-led culture that brands like PLT thrived on. The growing popularity of resale platforms further complicates PLT’s attempt to move toward longevity-focused fashion. As Collins noted, "Young shoppers are also pivoting more towards the resale market, as well as smaller capsule wardrobes." If PLT fails to meet the evolving demands of its audience, it risks alienating the customers it aims to retain. Despite the new branding’s lofty ambitions, Collins suggests that PLT might be struggling to justify its new higher price points. "PrettyLittleThing rebranded last week, attempting to reposition itself with more elevated, timeless styles. However, the reaction to this has been mostly negative, with the brand failing to justify its new higher price points with either improved quality or better environmental credentials," she said. A shift to higher-end fashion isn’t enough if the quality and sustainability don’t back it up, especially when more affordable, fast-moving brands like Shein continue to dominate with their ultra-low prices. As of this week, Boohoo has also made major moves. Just days ago, Boohoo Group announced it was rebranding to the Debenhams Group. The company, which acquired the struggling department store Debenhams in 2022, has been touting its turnaround as evidence of its future potential. Although Boohoo’s core youth-focused brands, such as Boohoo.com and BoohooMAN, are still under the group’s umbrella, it may be looking to align itself with a more established, perhaps older, demographic. Marcus Jaye, a fashion industry expert, said that the rebrand to Debenhams might be a deliberate move to target an older, more affluent customer base—particularly in light of rising competition from Shein and growing consumer concerns over sustainability. He said: "The model of buying lots and often of cheap product has been squeezed by new entries into the affordable fashion market. If consumers are buying less, you need them to spend more. " With younger shoppers turning to more sustainable options or choosing smaller, curated wardrobes, Boohoo might be repositioning itself to capture a more mature audience that is less price-sensitive but still seeks style and quality. However, like PLT, Boohoo Group's decision to distance itself from its previous branding could also be driven by the negative connotations that come with 'fast fashion'. Collins said: "Boohoo Group’s rebrand to become the Debenhams Group highlights how much its youth fast fashion brands—PrettyLittleThing, Boohoo.com, and BoohooMAN—continue to struggle." Despite the rebranding effort, Boohoo’s youth brands have seen a sharp decline in sales, with the group’s "GMV pre-returns plummeting 21.8%" in FY24/25. This dramatic decline suggests how deeply the fast-fashion model is struggling in the face of changing consumer habits and competition from other players in the market, including Shein. Collins blames the rise of Shein as one of the main reasons Boohoo’s brands have struggled. With Shein’s ability to offer ultra-low prices and a constant stream of new styles, it’s become almost impossible for traditional fast-fashion brands like Boohoo and PLT to keep up. The rebrands of PLT and Boohoo reveal an interesting crossroads for the fast-fashion industry. As demand for quick turnover, ultra-cheap clothing begins to dwindle, these brands are attempting to reposition themselves as more sustainable and sophisticated. But can they truly change their consumer perception, or will they forever be tied to the world of disposable, low-cost fashion? Retail expert Richard Hyman said: "Rebranding is different packaging that requires different contents to deliver the new promise. The two go hand in hand. Building a platform or marketplace model is something many big players did some years ago. I’m not saying they shouldn’t do it, but it’s just another door brands can sell through. Will it deliver more revenue for those brands? If so, where will it be captured from?" Hyman also noted a crucial perspective on the broader challenges facing the industry. He added: "Clothing is the hardest-hit market in a mature industry showing flat demand. So, any sales growth must come from someone else. What are they bringing to the party that is qualitatively better?" These are questions that Boohoo and PLT must answer as they attempt to reinvent themselves. "I think we need to have answers to these questions before judging whether this is a repackage or a more fundamental change", Hyman concluded. Collins was also skeptical of the success of these rebrands in the long term. She stressed that while Debenhams’ recent performance has been promising, "Boohoo Group’s rebrand is unlikely to reverse the decline of its youth brands overnight." The rebrands of PLT and Boohoo highlight the ongoing transformation of the fashion industry. As the demand for slower, more conscious fashion grows, brands that fail to evolve beyond their fast fashion origins may find themselves left behind. The question remains: Will these rebrands become the future of fast fashion, or will they simply be another attempt to polish a tarnished reputation? Time will tell.

article_title: PrettyLittleThing unveils rebrand as it moves away from fast fashion past
sub_title: PrettyLittleThing has unveiled its rebrand under the title of 'A Legacy in Progress', which promises to "redefine accessible luxury for...
article_content: PrettyLittleThing has unveiled its rebrand and relaunch under the title of 'A Legacy in Progress', which promises to "redefine accessible luxury for a new generation", while distancing the brand from its fast fashion past. Under the guidance of returning co-founder Umar Kamani, who re-joined PrettyLittleThing in September 2024 – marking a "new chapter" for the fashion giant following some turbulent times – the new direction points to a more sophisticated, longer lasting appeal. The "comprehensive elevation" touches every aspect of the new PrettyLittleThing experience – from elevated new collections to an inspiring digital destination. The focus is on two standout collections for the relaunch, PLT Label, "setting a new standard in contemporary elegance", and New Beginnings, "a sophisticated celebration of modern style". At the heart of the rebrand is a reimagining of PrettyLittleThing's visual identity. The distinctive unicorn emblem, once a playful symbol in bubblegum pink, has matured into a sophisticated, heritage-inspired mark that "marries the elegance of a historic coat of arms with modern design" in richer tones, while also "blending timeless heritage with a youthful edge." Kamani, who founded the business with his brother in 2012, said: "Fashion has incredible power to inspire, elevate and transform. A Legacy in Progress is more than a rebrand - it's a movement that celebrates our customers' evolving style. We're writing the next chapter of fashion history, and we're just getting started. "The rebrand is all about evolving with our customer who we feel has outgrown elements of what we had offered her. Reducing our offering has allowed us to produce more elevated styles in terms of design, quality and fit. "We are leaving ‘fast fashion’ as we currently know it behind and discouraging wearing items just once, we want to give our customer styles that she can wear again and again, that can be styled in several different ways. "There are no plans to introduce new categories at present, we are more focused on refreshing, refining and improving our current offering to ensure our product range has moved in the same way our customer has grown." An event to mark the brand’s transformation is set to take place at a "chic venue" regarded as one of Paris’s most celebrated celebrity haunts this week, during Paris Fashion Week. Further details of the event are, as yet, under wraps, but the concept is to showcase the new world of PrettyLittleThing with a "quiet luxury" sensibility – featuring subtle branding and a refined guest list that embodies the new forward thinking identity.
